SwiftUI on iOS, a web client, FastAPI and Postgres behind both.

items.title: PM Thinking Coach
items.summary: A tool for people entering product management from zero. A comprehensive skill map covering both product management and system design, helping you assess your competencies, identify knowledge gaps, and structure your skills. Short lessons explain key concepts, while practical exercises and real-world business simulations help you develop the mindset and problem-solving skills of a product manager
items.imageAlt: The Skills Map: 71 skill cards arranged in six sectors and three rings, with a red line marking how far the learner has got
items.tagline: The map of the profession, turned into a route you can walk from zero

sections.heading: What it is
paragraphs: Most learning resources for new product managers are libraries: piles of articles you’re expected to organize yourself. That works if you already know what you’re missing—which is exactly what beginners don’t.

PM Thinking Coach turns the map of the profession into a learning path. Two skill trees - Product Management and System Design cover 167 skills in total. Each skill is a focused card you can open, explore, and learn from. 

But learning doesn’t stop at reading. Every skill block ends with a gate: a realistic business scenario with incomplete information. You make a decision, explain your reasoning, and defend it in writing - building the judgment and structured thinking that real product management requires.
PM Thinking Coach runs on iOS with SwiftUI and in the browser, powered by a shared FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend. One account, one skill map, one learning experience across platforms.
sections.imageAlt: The Learn screen: six directions, the current block, and the next lesson on a black plate
sections.caption: Learn answers two questions and nothing else: which direction am I on, and what do I read next.

sections.heading: A gate, not a quiz
paragraphs:
This is the decision the entire product is built around. A multiple-choice test measures whether you remember the right answer. The job of a product manager is different: to make a defensible decision with incomplete information.

That’s why every gate gives you a company, a constraint, and a deadline. You decide what evidence to investigate, make the call, and then explain why you made it.

The scoring system reinforces this philosophy rather than simply encouraging it. The decision itself is worth 25 of 100 points, while rationale and communication account for 60. With a passing score of 70, choosing the “right” option isn’t enough—you have to demonstrate how you arrived at it. A content validator also rejects scenarios where a defensible alternative would score unfairly low, preventing single-answer questions from entering the corpus in the first place.
bullets: Every gate has at least two scenarios, each featuring a different company, so you can’t pass a retake by memorizing the answer.
Failure has no penalty. You lose no XP, nothing gets locked, and your result points directly to the lessons that could help you improve.
The server owns progression. Score, XP, and unlock status are determined server-side; the client only renders them. A UI bug can never unlock a gate prematurely.
sections.imageAlt: A gate scenario: a shift-scheduling company whose month-two churn has risen from 9% to 16%
sections.caption: A gate opens with a situation, not a question. The evidence you choose to look at is part of what is scored.

sections.heading: The lessons
paragraphs: A lesson is built around one idea, one practical model, and the point where that model stops working. Product management lessons take three to five minutes; system design lessons take twelve to fifteen. Within each domain, the same fictional company runs through every skill block, so examples build on each other instead of resetting with every lesson.

Lessons can also include an audio overview: a two-host conversation that explores the material in the style people have come to expect from tools like NotebookLM. It isn’t the lesson being read aloud - because written prose rarely makes good audio. The dialogue is generated once at build time and stored as a content file, where it can be reviewed, edited, and versioned like any other piece of content. The runtime never calls an AI model.

Generated content is validated rather than blindly trusted. An audio draft is rejected if it introduces a number or term that doesn’t appear in the lesson, turns into a one-person monologue, or simply quotes the source material verbatim. When a lesson changes, its audio overview is automatically marked as outdated rather than silently narrating an older version.
sections.imageAlt: A lesson page with its audio overview player and a summary card headed “The point”
sections.caption: A lesson, its audio overview, and the one thing to take away from it.

sections.heading: What is in it
paragraphs: The corpus is authored, not generated - and it’s complete. Both skill trees are fully published from day one.
bullets: Two complete skill trees: Product Management (18 blocks, 71 skills) and System Design (18 blocks, 96 skills), with the full map available from the start.
248 lessons, 36 gates, and 87 gate scenarios.
96 System Design exercises, intentionally formative: they award no XP, don’t affect progression, and show the reference reasoning even when submitted empty.
A 489-term glossary, with diagrams stored as structured data rather than images, allowing screen readers to access meaningful descriptions instead of inaccessible visuals.
Eight competencies tracked per learner, covering the core domains of the skill map plus communication and system design
sections.imageAlt: The Progress screen: level, XP, blocks passed, lessons read, and the eight competencies
sections.caption: Progress owns the numbers, so the other screens do not repeat them.

sections.heading: Where it stands
paragraphs:
Both skill trees are complete, and a full end-to-end traversal has been verified through the API.

The evaluator currently runs on a deterministic mock provider. It exercises the complete evaluation flow, but the coaching output is intentionally stubbed, and gate calibration against QA fixtures cannot be meaningfully validated until a real model provider is connected. That is the next, and deliberately final, implementation decision. Nothing else in the product is coupled to a specific model, so the provider can be swapped without changing the underlying product or assessment logic.
bullets: Defined the beta success metrics before launch: activation, time to first value, D7 repeat practice, and whether the feedback was useful

items.caption: The skill map, made interactive. The red frontier is the only colour on it — it marks exactly what you have covered.

items.title: Rae Health
items.meta: Product Manager Intern; Bristol, ME. June 2026 - September 2026
items.summary: Defined the first North Star metric and metric tree for a live clinical wearable platform, and pressure-tested the ROI model behind the growth strategy.
items.tagline: Giving a clinical wearable platform its first real baseline

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Worked on a live clinical wearable platform, defining foundational product metrics and using data analysis and customer research to validate the growth strategy.

sections.heading: What RAE is
paragraphs: RAE stands for Realize, Analyze, Engage. It is a wearable device and companion app designed to support people in recovery from substance use disorder. The wearable continuously monitors physiological signals, while machine learning models identify patterns associated with stress or potential craving. The app then provides interventions intended to help users de-escalate in the moment, rather than waiting until their next appointment.

The product serves three audiences: people in recovery, the treatment providers and care teams supporting them, and employers running wellness programs. The company is supported by the National Institutes of Health and UT Tyler, collaborates on research with UMass Medical School and Garmin, and holds two U.S. patents.
sections.imageAlt: The RAE Health site, showing the tagline “Realize. Analyze. Engage.” and the wearable band
sections.caption: Realize, Analyze, Engage — and the band that does the reading.

sections.heading: How the detection works
paragraphs: The wearable continuously measures accelerometry, skin conductance, skin temperature, and heart rate. Machine learning models analyze these signals to identify physiological patterns associated with stress and craving. When a relevant pattern is detected, the device vibrates and the app surfaces de-escalation tools, including guided breathing exercises, so support is available while the user is experiencing the state.
Detection is not entirely sensor-driven. Users can also log events manually, helping fill gaps in the data and providing labeled observations that can be used to evaluate and refine the models.
sections.imageAlt: The RAE app capturing a stress event step by step, next to a calendar of event trends
sections.caption: Capturing an event, and the trends it feeds.

sections.heading: What the published research says
paragraphs: The detection system has been evaluated in peer-reviewed research. The model identified stress with 76% accuracy and craving with 69% accuracy, with false-positive rates of 33% and 28%, respectively. Clients reported greater awareness of their own physiological and behavioral patterns, while providers saw potential for more personalized care.

This research provided the context for the product metrics work. A product whose value depends on detection being reliable enough to act on needs to establish what is actually happening in practice: how many patients are actively using the system, how consistently they are being monitored, how much usable data is being generated, and how often users or care teams respond to detected events.

The baseline analysis was designed to answer those questions.

sections.heading: What I did
bullets: Defined the company's first North Star metric and supporting metric tree (Reach → Activation → Retention → Clinical Engagement)
Analyzed event-level data (85 patients, ~91,000 detection events, 6 months) to compute the product's first measured baseline

Stress-tested the ROI model behind the company's growth strategy: traced each figure to source, formula, or "unverifiable", then recomputed break-even and reframed the claim before it reached prospects
Ran 6 customer interviews alongside usability studies to validate hypotheses before committing engineering capacity, and turned a gap in the acquisition funnel into a scoped backlog item
sections.imageAlt: The RAE app showing stress event intensity and event counts broken down by time of day
sections.caption: The analytics the baseline came out of: event intensity and counts by time of day.

items.tagline: Two client engagements, from stakeholder interviews to shipped tooling

sections.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Questrom Consulting Lab pairs graduate teams with companies on real problems on a fixed timeline. I ran two engagements, both with technology clients, covering stakeholder discovery, scoping, delivery and the hand-off at the end.

sections.heading: LinkSquares — mapping the back office
paragraphs: LinkSquares is a Boston company building AI-powered contract lifecycle management software, founded in 2015 and used by more than 1,200 customers including DraftKings, Wayfair and TIME. It has raised roughly $164M, including a $100M Series C in 2022.
Fast growth leaves a company buying tools faster than it retires them. The engagement was to find out what the business actually runs on, and where the same job was being paid for twice.
bullets: Mapped 150+ back-office systems across 9 departments through 8 stakeholder interviews
Built a systems-relationship tool that surfaced $700K in projected annual savings from redundant tooling
sections.imageAlt: The LinkSquares site, showing its contract management platform and customer logos
sections.caption: LinkSquares sells contract lifecycle management to legal teams at companies like DraftKings, TIME and Wayfair.

sections.heading: Sikich — an enterprise AI knowledge assistant
paragraphs: Sikich is a Chicago-based professional services firm founded in 1982, offering accounting, advisory, technology and managed services, and ranked 27th on Accounting Today's Top 100 firms.

A firm that size holds most of its expertise in documents and in people's heads. The engagement was to make that knowledge answerable — a retrieval-augmented assistant staff could ask directly, rather than a search box over a file share.
bullets: Led development of the enterprise AI knowledge assistant and its RAG solution
Coordinated project execution, technical workstreams, deliverables and stakeholder alignment across the engagement
sections.imageAlt: The Sikich site, with the headline “Turn complex challenges into simple solutions”
sections.caption: Sikich: accounting, advisory, technology and managed services, from Chicago.
